scope: Editorial review and evidence mapping, not certification alignment or physical/vendor execution.

items.name: Cisco CCNA
items.note: Networking fundamentals, addressing, switching and basic service diagnosis; compare the current provider objectives with your own evidence notebook.

items.name: Cisco CCNP Enterprise
items.note: Enterprise routing, services, security and automation are relevant practice areas; the course is not a complete exam-objective mapping.

items.name: Cisco CCNP Data Center
items.note: Fabric, compute, storage and automation topics have scoped models and guided vendor practice; actual target proficiency needs its own evidence.

items.name: Cisco CCIE Enterprise Infrastructure
items.note: Expert-level enterprise work needs integrated time-bounded configuration and troubleshooting on supported targets beyond written questions.

items.name: Cisco CCIE Data Center
items.note: Expert-level data-center work needs platform-specific integration and failure recovery; a conceptual capstone does not certify that performance.

items.name: VMware certifications
items.note: This original label is a broad family reference. Confirm the current Broadcom program, product version and assessment before planning preparation. The fetched portal exposed no detailed syllabus, so no requirements or alignment are asserted.

items.name: Linux certifications
items.note: Linux administration practice now includes permissions, processes, storage and recovery. Choose a specific provider assessment and compare its current objectives independently.

items.name: Ansible / Red Hat Automation
items.note: Automation practice covers versioned intent, validation and rollback. Confirm the chosen Red Hat track and product scope on the provider site; no prerequisites, price or exam equivalence are asserted here.

items.name: Logical network diagram
items.note: Show client and return paths, routed underlay and optional overlay; draw native FC storage separately from Ethernet. See workbook section 1.

items.name: Physical network diagram
items.note: Identify devices, ports, cable paths, NIC/HBA attachment, racks and power. Verify physical diversity rather than counting links. See workbook section 2.

items.name: IP addressing plan
items.note: Record nonoverlapping subnets, gateways, allocation owners and site scope; include IPv6 policy where applicable. See workbook section 3.

items.name: VLAN plan
items.note: Map VLAN membership, trunks and routed boundaries; a VLAN ID alone is not an authorization policy. See workbook section 4.

items.name: Routing design
items.note: Document route sources, policy, summarization assumptions, convergence evidence and return paths. See workbook section 5.

items.name: Firewall policy
items.note: Define source/destination/service identity, intended allows and denies, logging and stateful return behavior. See workbook section 6.

items.name: Data center rack design
items.note: Record rack units, weight/power/cooling limits, maintenance clearances and independent feeds; supplied dimensions need target validation. See workbook section 7.

items.name: Server design
items.note: Connect CPU/memory demand, placement, NIC/HBA attachment and survivor capacity to measured workload requirements. See workbook section 8.

items.name: Storage design
items.note: Show FC fabrics, zoning/masking, host multipath, data protection and supported array/controller failure behavior. See workbook section 9.

items.name: HA design
items.note: Name the failure set, remaining capacity and shared dependencies; HA is not a backup or complete site-recovery plan. See workbook section 10.

items.name: Monitoring design
items.note: Define user-facing signals, infrastructure diagnosis, alert ownership and operation when the monitored system is impaired. See workbook section 11.

items.name: Backup strategy
items.note: Retain independently protected usable copies, keys and restore evidence; a successful backup job is insufficient. See workbook section 12.

items.name: DR plan
items.note: Specify fencing, recovery point, dependencies, cutover validation, RTO/RPO measurements and failback ownership. See workbook section 13.

items.name: Automation strategy
items.note: Use versioned intent, validation, review, bounded apply and rollback with actual resulting-state checks. See workbook section 14.

items.name: Documentation
items.note: Maintain an indexed as-built package with owner, revision, assumptions, evidence, limits and handover actions. See workbook section 15.

items.name: Define the problem
items.note: State the affected user operation, scope, time and expected behavior. Distinguish impact from detection time.

items.name: Gather evidence
items.note: Capture bounded observations with provenance, timestamps and relevant configuration; protect secrets and retain uncertainty.

items.name: Identify the affected layer
items.note: Locate the failing boundary using evidence from both sides. Layer labels organize investigation but do not prove cause.

items.name: Build hypotheses
items.note: List plausible explanations and an observation that would disprove each; do not promote the latest change to root cause by chronology alone.

items.name: Test safely
items.note: Choose one bounded reversible test on an owned target, with baseline, stop condition and cleanup. Avoid competing changes.

items.name: Apply corrective action
items.note: Apply the reviewed repair or mitigation under one owner. Record exactly what changed and which revision can be restored.

items.name: Validate
items.note: Repeat the original operation and policy/data checks, then verify stability and cleanup. A green process is not sufficient.

items.name: Document root cause
items.note: Separate confirmed causes, contributing conditions and unresolved hypotheses. Assign corrective actions and verification dates; do not invent certainty.

items.name: Learn packet behavior
items.note: Begin with a small owned topology, a baseline, one controlled fault and a recovery notebook. Existing local labs provide a no-hardware path.

items.name: Cisco Packet Tracer
items.note: Packet Tracer is a teaching simulator. Use its legal distribution and document which features are simulated rather than treating its output as hardware evidence.

items.name: GNS3 or EVE-NG
items.note: Emulation platforms still require legitimate images, adequate host resources and an isolated management/network plan. Feature support follows the exact image.

items.name: Wireshark
items.note: Capture only traffic you are authorized to inspect. Record interface/filter/time scope and protect payloads; a capture startup message is not decoded packet evidence.

items.name: Linux VM
items.note: Use a disposable Linux guest or the documented WSL scope. Record kernel/distribution differences and snapshot/restore requirements before mutations.

items.name: Windows Server VM
items.note: Use an owned licensed/evaluation server under its actual terms. Domain/role operations remain guided; do not attach a practice domain or DHCP service to a shared network.

items.name: Operate an enterprise lab
items.note: Move to integrated virtual appliances only after individual mechanisms and rollback procedures are understood. Resource capacity and legal images are prerequisites.

items.name: Cisco IOSv / IOSvL2
items.note: IOSv/IOSvL2 are platform-specific virtual practice targets. Verify supported features and image rights; virtual behavior does not establish ASIC or physical-port behavior.

items.name: CSR1000v / Catalyst 8000V
items.note: These are original virtual-router family examples, not current purchase advice. Confirm the exact supported image/version and resource/license requirements.

items.name: NX-OSv
items.note: NX-OS virtual practice is feature- and version-scoped. Do not infer physical Nexus forwarding, vPC or storage capabilities from a generic VM.

items.name: FortiGate VM or equivalent firewall
items.note: Use an owned virtual firewall with explicit interfaces, allow/deny tests and rollback. Do not route normal host traffic through an unreviewed practice policy.

items.name: Windows Server / Ubuntu Server
items.note: Choose the OS required by the lesson and record its version. Keep identity, DNS/DHCP and routing experiments isolated from shared services.

items.name: VMware ESXi or equivalent hypervisor
items.note: Use a supported owned hypervisor and compatible hardware/software. Product licensing and trial availability are not assumed by this course.

items.name: Test real dependencies
items.note: Physical practice is optional and requires an owned target, maintenance access and an exact rollback plan. The educational curriculum does not claim these operations were executed.

items.name: Catalyst 2960X / 9200
items.note: The listed Catalyst families are historical roadmap examples. Validate lifecycle, software support and needed features before selecting any real target.

items.name: Cisco ISR4331
items.note: The listed ISR is a historical practice example. Check its exact support/release context; virtual routing results do not prove physical throughput.

items.name: Nexus 3K / 5K / 9K
items.note: Nexus families differ in features and lifecycle. Select a supported exact target and keep fabric, storage and management paths distinct.

items.name: Access point + wireless controller
items.note: Wireless practice needs permitted RF operation, compatible AP/controller software and client evidence. Wired reachability alone does not validate roaming or radio capacity.

items.name: HPE DL380 Gen9 / Gen10
items.note: These ProLiant generations are historical examples. Check firmware, OS compatibility, power and lifecycle for the owned unit; no purchase recommendation is made.

items.name: SAN storage + Brocade or Cisco SAN switch
items.note: SAN work needs precise WWPNs, supported zoning/masking/multipath and protected data. Never infer a safe LUN change from a hostname alone.

items.name: UPS + managed PDU
items.note: Power practice requires qualified personnel and approved procedures. Do not pull shared feeds or defeat protections to reproduce a classroom failure.

items.name: Internet
items.note: External users and dependencies are outside the local failure boundary; define reachability and provider assumptions.

items.name: ISP A
items.note: Provider A needs its own path and routing evidence; a name on a diagram does not prove physical diversity.

items.name: ISP B
items.note: Provider B can share ducts, exchanges or power with A; verify actual independence before claiming resilience.

items.name: Edge router A
items.note: Edge A needs policy, upstream and return-route validation under normal and failed states.

items.name: Edge router B
items.note: Edge B must have usable survivor capacity and policy, not merely a configured neighbor.

items.name: Firewall A
items.note: Firewall A enforces the explicit zone policy and contributes connection state to the HA design.

items.name: Firewall B
items.note: Firewall B needs supported state/policy synchronization and tested takeover behavior.

items.name: HA / state sync
items.note: A heartbeat or sync link alone does not prove equivalent policy or preservation of the original application session.

items.name: Redundant core pair
items.note: The core pair needs a documented topology and failure behavior; device count is insufficient.

items.name: Spine 1
items.note: Spine 1 participates in the routed underlay with links to the leaves; hosts are not implied to attach directly.

items.name: Spine 2
items.note: Spine 2 supplies an alternate fabric path only under the actual routing and failure design.

items.name: Leaf 1
items.note: Leaf 1 provides selected host/border attachment; map its exact NIC, uplink and policy relationships.

items.name: Leaf 2
items.note: Leaf 2 must be placed and connected according to the supported host multihoming design.

items.name: Leaf 3
items.note: Leaf 3 needs the same explicit underlay/overlay and port mapping, not a copied redundancy label.

items.name: Leaf 4
items.note: Leaf 4 contributes capacity and paths only where workloads and policy actually use it.

items.name: Server farm / VMware
items.note: Compute/hypervisor workloads depend on storage, identity, networking and management; validate actual placement and survivor capacity.

items.name: dual NIC attachment · vPC where supported
items.note: Dual NICs require a supported bonding/multihoming design. vPC is conditional, not a universal server requirement.

items.name: SAN A + SAN B
items.note: SAN A and SAN B are separate native FC fabrics. Shared arrays, software or power remain possible common failures.

items.name: host HBAs → FC fabrics → storage
items.note: Native FC attachment is host HBA to FC fabric to storage target; it is not an Ethernet-leaf cable in this reference.

items.name: Distribution / access
items.note: Campus distribution/access attaches users and local services through deliberate routed/policy boundaries.

items.name: campus + wireless
items.note: Wireless and campus access need their own client, RF, policy and failure observations.

items.name: Management / OOB
items.note: Management/OOB needs protected access and a path usable during production-network impairment.

items.name: AAA · DNS · DHCP · NTP
items.note: AAA, DNS, DHCP and time are distinct service dependencies; record identities, addressing, trust and recovery order.

items.name: Monitoring · Syslog
items.note: Monitoring and logs need protected retention, meaningful signals and access during incidents; telemetry success is not application success.

items.name: Automation server
items.note: Automation must use scoped authority, reviewed intent and validation/rollback; its host is itself a dependency.

items.name: NetBox · Ansible · Git
items.note: NetBox, Ansible and Git are example roles for inventory, execution and version history, not interchangeable sources of truth.

items.name: Backup / recovery
items.note: Backup/recovery includes usable protected copies, keys, restore procedure and data reconciliation.

items.name: independent copies
items.note: Independence means a different relevant failure/administration boundary, not merely a second filename.

items.name: DR site
items.note: A DR site requires capacity, data, identity, connectivity and writer ownership before cutover.

items.name: tested RTO / RPO
items.note: RTO/RPO are targets until measured under a declared exercise; the local restore duration is not whole-site recovery time.

items.name: Logical reference only. EVPN controls a VXLAN overlay over the routed leaf-spine underlay. ACI is an alternative fabric operating model. Fibre Channel storage uses separate SAN paths from host HBAs; the storage attachment above represents workload dependency.
items.note: The original caption already distinguishes routed underlay, optional EVPN/VXLAN, alternative ACI and separate native FC. Retain these boundaries and use the worked attachment map for implementation planning.

items.name: Your engineering deliverables
items.note: All fifteen engineering deliverables are worked in the existing capstone workbook; each still needs target-specific evidence before operational deployment.
